intro: Mahler follows the funeral march with an A-minor storm, torn open by a cello lament. Near the end, the brass find a magnificent D-major chorale — and lose it again.

sections.label: A · Running basses and slashing chords
sections.mNote: Low strings hurl a five-note figure against orchestral blows

sections.label: B · Cellos recall the funeral march
sections.mNote: Four flats, at the first movement’s tempo

sections.label: A′ · The running strings return
sections.mNote: The opening figures break back into the cello lament

sections.label: B′ · Cellos over a timpani roll
sections.mNote: A long E♭-minor song with scarcely any accompaniment

sections.label: Dev · March and storm collide
sections.mNote: A faster march in a major key, then the storm returns

sections.label: C · Brass chorale in D major
sections.mNote: Long brass chords above racing strings and harp

sections.label: Coda · The storm returns in scraps
sections.mNote: Short string figures survive the fading brass chorale

cues.title: A five-note figure, then a blow
cues.text: Cellos, basses and bassoons open at fff with a five-note figure that climbs two steps and falls back. A rit. holds it up before each hard orchestral chord; Mahler’s footnote says the pause only gathers force, and the figure itself stays fast. The marking is Mit grösster Vehemenz: with the greatest vehemence.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 48: Stürmisch bewegt. Mit grösster Vehemenz.; the figure in bassoons, cellos and basses marked fff with rit. and a tempo; the conductor’s footnote ends “Die Figur selbst muss im schnellen Tempo ausgeführt werden.” Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide describes the opening as motivic fragments, descending lines, harsh dissonances and a loud dynamic: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cellos remember the march
cues.text: The rapid woodwind notes run out, leaving a timpani roll. At rehearsal 5 Mahler writes Bedeutend langsamer (im Tempo des ersten Satzes “Trauermarsch”) — much slower, in the tempo of the funeral march — and the cellos begin a lament marked molto cantando, in four flats.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 57–58, rehearsal 5: timpani roll mf to pp; Bedeutend langsamer (im Tempo des ersten Satzes „Trauermarsch“); cellos molto cantando, four flats. Basinger: the lyrical cello melody enters in the tempo of the first movement’s funeral march, molto cantando, in a minor key: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song is passed on
cues.text: The cello song is taken up and answered. Clarinets add a counter-melody marked etwas hervortretend, slightly to the fore, and the first violins sing the tune marked zart, tender, over plucked strings.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 58: bass clarinet and clarinets etwas hervortretend, espress.; p. 60: first violins (zart) over pizzicato violas, cellos and basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two summers at Maiernigg
cues.text: Mahler begins the Fifth in the summer of 1901. By the time he returns to Maiernigg the next summer, he has met and married Alma Schindler, and they are expecting their first child. The symphony takes shape across those two summers.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction: composition in 1901–02 and the family chronology. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: The storm cuts the song short
cues.text: The opening figure comes back in cellos, basses and bassoons at ff, with horns stopped and trumpets muted, and the development begins in the storm’s old manner.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 66: the figure in bassoons, contrabassoon, cellos and basses ff; horns gestopft, trumpets mit Dämpfer. Basinger: the development reintroduces the turbulent mood of the Stürmisch bewegt and its motives: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cellos over a timpani roll
cues.text: Marked pp klagend am Griffbrett — plaintive, bowed near the fingerboard — the cellos return to their song in E♭ minor. A timpani roll runs beneath, and the violas hold one long note; almost nothing else accompanies them.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 70–71: rit., then six flats and Langsam aber immer; cellos pp klagend am Griffbrett, timpani roll throughout, violas am Griffbrett on a sustained note. Basinger: the cello melody returns marked klagend above an ominous timpani roll: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horns take the song
cues.text: At rehearsal 12 Mahler returns to Tempo moderato (wie im ersten Teil). Two horns, marked espress. and zart hervortretend, sing the melody over rapid repeated notes in flutes, clarinets and bassoons.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 71, rehearsal 12: Tempo moderato (wie im ersten Teil); horns espress., zart hervortretend over repeated notes in the woodwinds. Basinger: the music after the klagend return varies the cello melody and combines it with material from the Trauermarsch: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Published, then revised
cues.text: Peters publishes the Fifth in 1904, and a second edition in 1905 carries Mahler’s revisions of 1904. His last corrections, made in 1911, reach print only in 1964.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page for the symphony gives the 1904 and 1905 Peters editions and the 1911 revisions printed in 1964: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/ . The Aspen Music Festival programme note says Mahler kept touching up the scoring almost until he died: https://www.aspenmusicfestival.com/program_notes/view/mahler-symphony-no.-5-in-c-sharp-minor

cues.title: The funeral march learns to march
cues.text: Mahler marks the change Più mosso subito, aber immer noch nicht so schnell wie zu Anfang — suddenly faster, though still not as fast as at the start. The mournful music turns into a march in a major key, and it gains in intensity as it goes.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 78, rehearsal 16: Più mosso subito, aber immer noch nicht so schnell wie zu Anfang. Basinger: the composer brusquely switches to a faster-moving march in a major key that gains in intensity: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A new day, briefly
cues.text: The march broadens into a brass chorale over a ringing triangle, with dramatic punctuation from the timpani. It cannot hold. The stormy motives of the opening break in and the movement starts over.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the march broadens into a brass chorale resounding over a ringing triangle with dramatic timpani punctuation; unable to sustain itself, it gives way as the stormy motives intrude and the recapitulation begins: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/

cues.title: The brass find D major
cues.text: At the movement’s high point the brass sustain long chords in D major, two sharps. Strings sweep upward in rushing scales and the harp adds rising runs at fff, with cymbals struck mit Teller. D major is the key in which the symphony will end.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 102: two sharps; horns, trumpets and trombones on sustained chords; harp fff rising runs; Becken mit Teller; rushing scales in violins, violas, cellos and basses. Basinger: the movement reaches an extended peak in a D-major chorale, a key with significant implications for the rest of the symphony: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The storm has survived
cues.text: The chorale fades: Mahler marks Ritenuto, the brass chords die away to pp, and the strings sink to morendo. The stormy opening motives come back for the coda. The D-major hymn will have to wait until the finale to close the symphony.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 107: Ritenuto, diminuendo in the brass, harp arpeggios, strings morendo. Basinger: the Stürmisch bewegt motives resurface as the coda begins and prove short-lived (second movement); a chorale from this movement returns at the high point of the finale (fifth movement): https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Harp notes in the wreckage
cues.text: The last pages scatter wind and harp notes among pale string chords. The cellos and basses pluck a final ppp figure, the timpani sound one last soft note, and Mahler adds folgt lange Pause — a long pause follows.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 116–117: sparse wind, harp and triangle notes over divided strings; last bars poco rit., cellos and basses Tutti pizz. ppp, timpani p (gut stimmen!), “(folgt lange Pause.)”. Basinger: the anguished sigh remains until the composer silences it: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A timpani roll, then the cellos
transitions.from: A · Running basses and slashing chords
transitions.to: B · Cellos recall the funeral march
transitions.how: The woodwinds’ racing notes dwindle to a stop over a timpani roll that fades to pp. At rehearsal 5 Mahler slows to the first movement’s funeral-march tempo, in four flats, and the cellos sing molto cantando.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 57–58: Sehr drängend, timpani roll mf to pp, rehearsal 5 Bedeutend langsamer (im Tempo des ersten Satzes „Trauermarsch“), cellos molto cantando.

transitions.title: The woodwinds bring back the storm
transitions.from: B · Cellos recall the funeral march
transitions.how: The song is cut off. The opening figure returns in cellos, basses and bassoons at ff, with horns stopped and trumpets muted, and the stormy music takes over again.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 66: the opening figure in bassoons, contrabassoon, cellos and basses ff; horns gestopft, trumpets mit Dämpfer. Basinger: the development reintroduces the turbulent mood and its motives.

transitions.title: The timpani roll stays behind
transitions.to: B′ · Cellos over a timpani roll
transitions.how: The storm winds down at a rit. and a timpani roll takes over. Six flats arrive with Langsam aber immer, and the cellos begin a slower E♭-minor song, pp klagend am Griffbrett, with the violas holding a long note beneath.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 70–71: rit., change to six flats, Langsam aber immer, cellos pp klagend am Griffbrett, timpani roll, violas am Griffbrett.

transitions.title: D major opens above the strings
transitions.to: C · Brass chorale in D major
transitions.how: D major arrives in sustained brass chords. The strings rush upward in scales, the harp adds rising runs, and cymbals are struck with a plate.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 102: two sharps, sustained chords in horns, trumpets and trombones, harp fff runs, Becken mit Teller, rushing string scales.

transitions.title: Short figures invade the chorale
transitions.from: C · Brass chorale in D major
transitions.to: Coda · The storm returns in scraps
transitions.how: At Ritenuto the D-major brass chords subside to pp, the harp adds a few plucked arpeggios and the strings sink to morendo. The stormy opening motives return for the coda and thin out until almost nothing is left.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 107: Ritenuto, brass diminuendo to pp, harp arpeggios, strings morendo. Basinger: the Stürmisch bewegt motives resurface as the coda begins and prove short-lived.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, II, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed p. 48: rushing low strings and orchestral attacks; pp. 57–58: slow cello melody; p. 102: brass chorale; pp. 107–116: withdrawal and coda.

timeline.note: Running low strings and bassoons meet sharp orchestral attacks.
The woodwind figures soften above held notes in the lower instruments.
Cellos sing the slower melody, with sparse woodwinds and bass punctuation.
The brass chorale opens above moving strings and harp.
Brass chords and low instruments fade after the chorale.
Quiet upper strings, scraps of woodwind melody and isolated harp notes finish the movement.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
